name: Jüdisch-palästinisches Aramäisch, galiläischer und targumischer Dialekt = Jewish Palestinian Aramaic, Galilean and Targumic dialects
confidence_why: Dalman 1905, Stevenson 1924, Marshall 1929 and Riggs 1858 (after Winer) all state that the Galilean and Targumic dialects stress the final syllable and differ only over which morphological forms are penultimate exceptions, while the penultimate rules of Petermann 1873 and of the Ashkenazi reading tradition concern Samaritan Aramaic and a later European pronunciation, not these dialects.

catalog_quote: 5. Da die in Ausg. Sab. durchgeführte Akzentuation nicht für die jemenischen Texte maßgebend ist, kann nur aus der Vokalisation selbst erkannt werden, wo der Wortakzent im targum. Dialekt seine Stelle hatte. Dasselbe gilt vom galil. Dialekt, dessen unvollkommene Vokalisation freilich nicht immer sichere Schlüsse zuläßt. Bei beiden Dialekten spricht der Tatbestand für vorwiegende Betonung der Ultima, womit auch das Zeugnis des bibl. Aramäisch und der praktischen Lesetradition der Jemaniten übereinstimmt. Die dem Dialekt von Ma'lula eigene vorwiegende Betonung der Paenultima war also hei [sic, = bei] den palästinischen Juden nicht üblich. Nur in folgenden Fällen ist Betonung der Paenultima anzunehmen: a. im galil. und targum. Dialekt: α. bei katl-, kitl-, kutl-Bildungen, wenn in der indet. oder Verbindungsform die hebraisierende Aussprache angewandt ist ... (§ 25). β. bei den Adverbien mit lokativer Akkusativendung ... (§ 44). b. im galil. Dialekt: α. bei den Nominalsuffixen am Plural ... (§ 41). β. bei dem Verbalsuffix ... (§ 76). γ. im Perfekt des starken Verbum bei der 2. P. Sg. mit ה und der 1. P. Pl. aller Stämme ... (§ 60); bei den Verben tertiae א, ו, י in der 2. P. Sg. auf ā, der 1. P. Sg. auf ī, und in der 1. P. Pl. des Perfekts ... (§ 72). δ. in der (wohl eigentlich einsilbigen) Endung ין des Plur. masc. der Participia der Verba tertiae א, ו, י ... (§ 72), auch im Worte מין (§ 40).

new_statements.translation: 5. Since the accentuation carried through in the Sabbioneta edition is not authoritative for the Yemenite texts, where the word accent lay in the Targumic dialect can only be recognized from the vocalization itself. The same holds for the Galilean dialect, whose imperfect vocalization admittedly does not always permit secure conclusions. In both dialects the facts speak for predominant stress on the ultima, with which the testimony of Biblical Aramaic and of the practical reading tradition of the Yemenites also agrees. The predominant penultimate stress peculiar to the dialect of Ma'lula was thus not usual among the Palestinian Jews. Only in the following cases is penultimate stress to be assumed: ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jewish Palestinian Aramaic (Galilean dialect of the Palestinian Talmud/Midrashim and the Targumic dialect): word stress predominantly on the final syllable; penultimate stress only in a closed list of morphological categories.
new_statements.exceptions: Penult stress assumed (pp. 55-56): (a) Galilean+Targumic: qatl/qitl/qutl segolates in Hebraizing indet./construct pronunciation; locative adverbs with accusative -ā (e.g. 'above', 'below', 'here'); (b) Galilean: plural nominal suffixes and -n on vowel-final singulars; verbal suffix -nī type; perfect 2sg in -tā and 1pl of all stems, 3fs of stems with e in last syllable, III-weak 2sg -tā/1sg -tī/1pl; mpl participle ending -yin of III-weak verbs and the word mayin; (c) Targumic: pronouns ('we' etc.), various nominal and verbal suffixes, perfect 3fs, 2sg -tā, 1sg, 3pl m/f, 1pl, imperative fs and pl, III-weak forms, endings -ayin. Stevenson 1924 p.15 and Marshall 1929 pp.29-30 repeat the final-stress rule with similar exception lists.
new_statements.domain_note: Word accent of extinct written varieties, inferred from vocalized manuscripts (Yemenite supralinear Targum MSS; sporadic vocalization of Galilean texts) and the Yemenite reading tradition; the printed Sabbioneta accent marks are explicitly discounted. Applies to the Jewish Palestinian dialects only. The Samaritan dialect of the same Glottolog language is described with the opposite rule: Petermann 1873 p. 6 § 9 (file) 'Tonus.. penultimam syllabam semper ferit' (penult always, except letter names and prefixed monosyllables), from the living Samaritan recitation; modern Samaritan grammars (Macuch 1982, Ben-Hayyim, Tal 2013) are reported to agree, and Ben-Hayyim/Kutscher extended a penultimate-stress hypothesis to Galilean and Christian Palestinian Aramaic, so the languoid-level picture is dialect-split and debated.
new_statements.identity_note: late1255 is a Glottolog language-level umbrella over three written Late Antique/medieval Western Aramaic varieties. The quoted statement (Dalman 1905) covers only the Jewish Palestinian dialects: Galilean Aramaic (gali1269, Palestinian Talmud/Midrash) and the 'Targumic' dialect (Onkelos in Yemenite MSS + Palestinian Targums; Glottolog pale1261 [jpa]) -> predominantly FINAL stress. The Samaritan dialect (sama1314 [sam]) is described first-hand with PENULTIMATE stress (Petermann 1873 p. 6 § 9, saved), and modern Samaritanists (Macuch 1982, Ben-Hayyim, Tal 2013; not opened) are the authorities for that. No stress statement was readable for Christian Palestinian Aramaic (chri1239). A catalog entry keyed to late1255 should either be split by dialect or flagged as dialect-divergent (JPA final vs Samaritan penult), and note that Ben-Hayyim/Kutscher-era scholarship disputes Dalman's final-stress reading for Galilean.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (fixed final) and as Dalman 1905 § 9.5 for the Targumic dialect; adds the three explicit exception classes and the note that the Ashkenazi reading tradition is penultimate. Riggs describes Biblical Aramaic and the Babylonian-vocalized Targums (Onkelos/Jonathan), i.e. the 'Targumic dialect' side of the catalog entry plus Biblical Aramaic; he says nothing about the Galilean dialect, and the Samaritan appendix (pp. 151ff) contains no statement on accent.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word tone (stress) in 'Chaldee' — Riggs's term for Biblical Aramaic plus the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan — falls, as in Tiberian Hebrew, usually on the last syllable. Penultimate stress is an exception restricted to three morphological classes: Hebrew-type segholate nouns (mostly in Biblical Aramaic), verbal forms with certain vocalic endings (e.g. 3fs/3pl perfect endings, the -nā endings), and certain pronominal suffixes. He adds that the Ashkenazi (German and Polish) reading tradition puts the tone on the penult and that the ancient Babylonian accentuation cannot be recovered from Syriac.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the half-accent Metheg is only mentioned as used less regularly than in Hebrew (§ 2.9.a, p. 20).
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate: (1) segholate nouns following the Hebrew pattern (almost only in Biblical Chaldee); (2) verbal forms ending in certain suffixes (the scanned garbles the Hebrew, the classes are the perfect endings -at/-ā, -nā, -tā etc.); (3) certain pronominal suffixes. Also: Ashkenazi readers place the tone on the penult throughout. Passim: tone 'thrown forward' by suffixes (§ 8, § 22) and 'penultimate' tone in the emphatic state of some nouns.
new_statements.identity_note: Riggs's 'Chaldee' = Biblical Aramaic (Daniel, Ezra) plus the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan (and Jerusalem Targum selections in the chrestomathy), i.e. Dalman's 'targumischer Dialekt' together with Biblical Aramaic (Glottolog would put the latter under Imperial/Biblical Aramaic, not late1255); he says nothing about the Galilean dialect. Schulthess 1924 (not opened) describes Christian Palestinian Aramaic (chri1239).

new_statements.relation_note: First edition; the tone-syllable section is verbatim the same as in the 1858 fourth edition (the 1832 appendix covers only Rabbinic, no Samaritan section). Agrees with the catalog's final stress and with Dalman's statement for the Targumic dialect; describes Biblical Aramaic + Targums (Onkelos/Jonathan), not the Galilean dialect.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Identical statement to the 1858 edition: tone usually on the final syllable, as in Hebrew; penultimate in Hebrew-type segholates, in verbal forms with certain endings, and with certain suffixes; Ashkenazi readers use penultimate tone.
new_statements.exceptions: Same three penultimate classes as the 1858 edition (segholate nouns, certain verbal endings, certain suffixes); Ashkenazi penult reading tradition.
new_statements.identity_note: Riggs's 'Chaldee' = Biblical Aramaic (Daniel, Ezra) plus the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan (and Jerusalem Targum selections in the chrestomathy), i.e. Dalman's 'targumischer Dialekt' together with Biblical Aramaic (Glottolog would put the latter under Imperial/Biblical Aramaic, not late1255); he says nothing about the Galilean dialect. Schulthess 1924 (not opened) describes Christian Palestinian Aramaic (chri1239).

readall_conflicts: Riggs (both editions) reports that German and Polish (Ashkenazi) Jews read Chaldee with penultimate tone, but presents this as a reading tradition and explicitly leaves the ancient accentuation undecided; his grammatical rule is ultima. The earlier reading's Petermann 1873 penultimate rule concerns the Samaritan Aramaic reading tradition (sama1314), a different dialect under the late1255 node, and is not a statement about the Jewish Galilean/Targumic dialects. Schulthess 1924 (Christian Palestinian Aramaic) could not be opened.
